back: A straight-line graph used to convert between two units, such as US dollars and rand.

front: When does a conversion graph pass through the origin?
back: When the two quantities are in direct proportion (zero of one is zero of the other), e.g. currencies, km and miles.

front: Does the Celsius-Fahrenheit graph pass through the origin?
What does the gradient of a straight-line real-life graph represent?
back: A rate of change, in vertical units per horizontal unit (e.g. litres per minute).

front: What does a negative gradient mean on a real-life graph?
back: The vertical quantity is decreasing, e.g. a dam level falling by $0.1$ m per day.

front: What does the vertical intercept often represent in a cost graph?
back: A fixed charge, such as a set-up or call-out fee, paid even when nothing is used.

front: Which quantity goes on the horizontal axis?
back: The controlled (independent) quantity, often time; the measured quantity goes up the side.

front: Water flows at a constant rate into a cylinder. Shape of the depth-time graph?
Water flows at a constant rate into a container that widens upwards. Shape of the depth-time graph?
back: A curve that becomes less steep (the depth rises more slowly).

front: How should you read a value from a graph in an exam?
back: Draw ruled reading lines from the axis to the graph and across (or down) to the other axis, and state the value.
